abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational paradigm for geometric filtering based on persistent homology gradients, fundamentally shifting how discrete geometric structures are analyzed and classified. Traditional approaches rely on combinatorial topology or metric-based techniques, which often struggle with noise robustness and scale invariance. Our framework, termed Homological Gradient Descent (HGD), treats geometric features as critical points in the persistence diagram landscape and evolves candidate solutions through gradient flows defined on the space of geometric configurations. We prove that HGD converges to locally optimal geometric realizations in O(n log n) iterations under mild regularity conditions, with each iteration requiring only constant-time updates to the filtration. The paradigm naturally extends to high-dimensional settings without combinatorial explosion, as the core operations are defined on algebraic topology constructs rather than explicit simplicial complexes. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets demonstrates that HGD achieves superior classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining theoretical guarantees on geometric optimality. This work opens new research directions by bridging computational topology with continuous optimization, potentially impacting fields ranging from geometric modeling to mesh generation where robust feature extraction is essential.

We present a significantly improved algorithm for computing the Euclidean minimum spanning tree (EMST) in d-dimensional point sets, achieving a time complexity of O(n log n + n ⌈d/2⌉) compared to the previous best bound of O(n^(2-1/⌈d/2⌉) + n log n). The improvement stems from a novel application of the Matoušek's range searching framework combined with a carefully designed geometric partitioning scheme that exploits the convex geometry underlying the EMST structure. Our key insight is that the critical edges in any d-dimensional EMST are contained within a sparse subset of the Delaunay graph, and we can identify this subset using efficient approximate nearest neighbor structures. We provide a complete analysis showing that our algorithm reduces the practical exponent of the high-dimensional term from approximately 1/2 to a logarithmic factor, making it the first practical improvement for dimensions d ≥ 4. For the special case of planar point sets (d=2), we further optimize the constants to achieve a near-linear algorithm with minor preprocessing. The theoretical improvements are validated through comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating speedups of up to three orders of magnitude for moderate-dimensional instances.

We present TopoMesh, a novel system for interactive mesh generation that leverages advances in computational topology to provide theoretically guaranteed mesh quality. Unlike traditional mesh generators that rely solely on geometric heuristics, TopoMesh integrates persistent homology analysis directly into the mesh refinement process to detect and eliminate geometric and topological defects before they propagate. The system architecture comprises three main components: (1) a streaming geometry processor capable of handling point clouds at 10^8 points per second, (2) an on-the-fly topological analyzer that maintains persistent barcodes during element insertion and deletion, and (3) an adaptive refinement engine that prioritizes geometric optimization while respecting topological constraints. The refinement decisions are guided by a multi-objective function balancing element quality, size gradation, and topological simplicity. We demonstrate TopoMesh's effectiveness on complex industrial geometries including turbine blades, urban terrain models, and organic anatomical structures. The system produces meshes with element quality metrics exceeding 0.9 on average while maintaining correct topology, achieving what prior systems could not accomplish. TopoMesh is released as an open-source library with bindings for Python and C++, enabling integration into existing computational geometry workflows.

This paper presents SubDiv++: a substantially improved subdivision surface system that achieves an order of magnitude speedup over existing implementations while maintaining theoretical optimality guarantees. The core innovation lies in a hierarchical spatial indexing structure that reduces the computational geometry overhead of neighborhood queries during subdivision from O(n) to O(log n) per vertex. Our system builds upon the theoretical foundation of Catmull-Clark subdivision but introduces adaptive weighted masks that depend on local mesh topology, computed efficiently using our novel local structure tensor. We prove that SubDiv++ preserves all desirable theoretical properties including C^2 continuity away from extraordinary vertices and C^1 continuity globally. The implementation employs GPU acceleration for batch processing of vertices, achieving real-time subdivision rates exceeding 100 million vertices per second on modern hardware. We provide extensive benchmarking on diverse geometric modeling scenarios including character animation, architectural surfaces, and reverse engineering applications. Results demonstrate that SubDiv++ produces visually indistinguishable outputs compared to traditional methods while running 12x faster on average, with the greatest improvements observed for meshes with high vertex counts or complex topology. The system includes a complete geometric modeling API supporting standard operations and file format interoperability.
